story: Palamedes was a prince, son of a king, who joined the Greeks in their expedition against Troy. He was credited with inventing dice, numbers, and letters. When Paris took Helen to Troy, the Greek leader sent word to all the kings to honor their oaths and defend the marriage. One king, wishing to avoid the war, feigned madness by yoking a donkey and an ox together to plow his fields, causing the plow to move chaotically. Palamedes, realizing the deception, placed the man's infant son in front of the plow, forcing him to swerve and reveal his sanity. This act showed Palamedes' cleverness and began a rivalry between the two men. Palamedes later fought alongside other heroes, killing a son of a war god, and stood his ground in battle to conquer a city after another great warrior was wounded and retreated. Accounts differ on his death: in one, his rival hid gold in his tent and forged a letter implicating him in treason, leading the Greeks to stone him to death. In another, he was drowned by two men during a fishing trip. In yet another, he was lured into a well seeking treasure and crushed with stones. In a different version, instead of dying early, he convinced the Greeks to make him their leader instead of the original commander, killed two enemy warriors in battle, but was then shot in the neck and killed by an enemy archer. He was remembered for his wisdom, his invention of counting and writing, and for the injustice of his death.

When a foreign prince took a queen to his city, the alliance's leader sent word to all the allied kings to honor their oaths and defend the marriage. One king, wishing to avoid the war, feigned madness by yoking two different pack animals together to plow his fields, causing the plow to move chaotically.
